title: A Spare Helmet and Three Weeks' Training: SafeBoda's Kampala Start
dek: In late 2014 a Kampala rider who had lost a friend to a crash, and two partners working in Rwanda, bet that safe boda rides could pay their way.

story.founder: Ricky Rapa Thomson, Maxime Dieudonné, Alastair Sussock
story.event: Starting SafeBoda with Red Cross-trained riders carrying passenger helmets in Kampala
story.summary: SafeBoda began in Kampala in November 2014, founded by former boda boda rider Ricky Rapa Thomson, who had started carrying a spare passenger helmet after a friend died in a crash, with Maxime Dieudonné and Alastair Sussock, then working in Rwanda. Riders trained with the Uganda Red Cross, carried a passenger helmet and charged ordinary fares; there were 50 riders by March 2015 and more than a thousand by 2017, though the early apps struggled. SafeBoda stopped rides in Nairobi in November 2020, citing Covid-19, and returned there for deliveries in 2024.
paragraphs: Ricky Rapa Thomson had come to Kampala alone, with no relatives to fall back on. He worked as a security guard at a Makerere University hostel and then as a boda boda rider. When a close friend he worked with was killed in a boda accident, he told The Observer in 2019, "once I lost him, I realized something needed to be done." He began carrying a spare helmet for passengers and persuaded other riders to do the same.

In 2014 Maxime Dieudonné, then working in Rwanda with Alastair Sussock, visited Kampala and was struck by how disorderly its boda trade looked beside Rwanda's, and how few people wore helmets. A mutual friend introduced him to Rapa. Dieudonné suggested an app; Rapa said later he had no idea how that would work. Dieudonné and Sussock took the overnight bus from Kigali to meet him and Moses Musinguzi, a rider who would wear helmet SB 1. The first office was one room in Kyebando.

They knew what they were up against. A Makerere University study at Mulago, the national referral hospital, had linked about 40 per cent of its trauma cases to boda crashes, and a 2004 law requiring helmets was widely ignored. Rather than wait for enforcement, they tried to make safety pay. Riders trained for up to three weeks with the Uganda Red Cross, wore orange vests, carried a helmet for the passenger and charged ordinary fares. Sussock called it "a market-based approach to road safety." By March 2015, four months after starting, there were 50 riders. Rapa told CNN that training would save lives, "But implementing has been a challenge."

It was. The founders later admitted their early apps were "crappy", and until a rebuilt one arrived in February 2017 most rides were still hailed on the street. Most passengers turned the helmet down, worried about hygiene or their hair. More than a thousand riders had joined, and MIT Technology Review reported no rider or passenger deaths since the 2014 launch. SafeBoda reached Nairobi in 2018. In November 2020, saying Covid-19 had hit boda transport hard, it stopped rides there; Kenyan reports put the riders affected at between hundreds and about 4,000. It returned to Nairobi for deliveries in 2024.

quote.text: Practise thyself even in the things which thou despairest of accomplishing. For even the left hand, which is ineffectual for all other things for want of practice, holds the bridle more vigorously than the right hand; for it has been practised in this.
quote.source_title: Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #15877
quote.connection: For years SafeBoda kept practising what it was still doing badly: persuading passengers into helmets, moving riders onto an app that barely worked. Marcus, writing of the left hand that grips the reins better than the right, suggests that strength in a weak place comes from that repetition, not from talent.

reflection: What held SafeBoda together in its first years was not the app. The technology was weak for more than two years. What carried the company was plainer: a spare helmet, three weeks of training, ordinary fares, and a rider who had decided after his friend's death that something had to change. The clever part came later; the patient part came first.

You probably have a left hand of your own, a skill you avoid because you are not good at it yet: asking for money, explaining your work to a stranger, stopping at a sensible hour. Marcus does not promise it will become easy. He only notes that the hand which has done the work before is the one that holds the reins.
invitation: Pick one task you have been avoiding because you do it badly. Give it fifteen minutes this morning, without trying to finish it, and stop when the time is up.

cross_checks.claim: SafeBoda began in Kampala in 2014 (CNN: inception in November 2014)
Rapa, a boda rider, lost a close friend in a motorcycle accident and began offering passengers a helmet
The model: riders trained with the Red Cross, carrying a passenger helmet, charging ordinary fares
About 40 per cent of trauma cases at Mulago hospital were linked to boda boda accidents
SafeBoda stopped rides in Kenya from 27 November 2020, citing Covid-19

research_notes: Slate said the Kenya exit was in 2022; contemporary reports (Nation, Business Daily, TechCabal) date the announcement to 16-17 November 2020 and the end of rides to 27 November 2020, so the story uses 2020. The episode told is the founding and first riders (late 2014 to early 2015), with the Kenya pause as part of what followed, so arc is founding-decision rather than the slate's change-of-direction. Start date: CNN (March 2015) gives inception in November 2014 and MIT Technology Review gives a 2014 launch; The Observer (2019) says operations 'started officially in 2015'. The story uses November 2014 for the start and says four months before March 2015. Riders affected in Kenya: Nation and Business Daily say hundreds of riders and staff would lose jobs while noting a network of more than 4,000 riders in Nairobi; TechCabal estimated 4,000 riders would lose their jobs. The story gives the range. Helmet uptake figures conflict and the story avoids them: MIT Technology Review (2017) said more than 60 per cent of passengers declined helmets; NPR (2018) reported uptake of about 30 per cent; Rapa told The Observer in 2019 that 60-70 per cent of customers wore them. The story says only that most passengers declined helmets in 2017. Mulago trauma share: CNN says approximately 40 per cent of trauma cases; MIT Technology Review says an estimated 41 per cent of trauma-ward admissions; the story says about 40 per cent. Dispatch: the 2025 anniversary piece says the first dispatcher used GPS, while The Observer (2019) says GPS was a challenge and an intermediate app routed requests through a call centre for manual dispatch; the story mentions only the one-room office. The Observer's 2025 'SafeBoda@10' piece and the Matooke Republic article share near-identical wording and read as a company-supplied anniversary account, so they are treated as one company source for the overnight bus, the Kyebando office and Moses Musinguzi as helmet SB 1, and are not relied on as independent of each other. MIT Technology Review names the founders' countries as the UK, Belgium and Uganda without assigning them, so the story does not give Dieudonné's or Sussock's nationality. Funding is venture: MIT Technology Review reports over $1 million in seed capital by 2017, and later investors are named in the anniversary account. Rapa's quotation keeps the source's US spelling 'realized'. The founding's later regulatory and Nigeria history are left out; Business Daily dates Nigeria entry to May 2020 while the anniversary account says 2018-19.
